Malavaggo

250 For whom this <term>asava</term> <gloss>intoxicant/taint</gloss> is cut off, uprooted, and pulled out, he truly attains <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>concentration</gloss> by day or by night.
8 The Story of the Young Monk Tissa, III 357

251 There is no fire like lust, no hold like hatred, no net like delusion, no river like craving.
9 The Story of the Five Lay Followers, III 360

252 The faults of others are easy to see, but one's own are difficult to see. A person winnows the faults of others like chaff, but hides his own faults like a crafty gambler hiding a losing die.
10 The Story of the Banker Meṇḍaka, III 363

253 For one who constantly observes the faults of others and is always finding fault, his taints grow; he is far from the destruction of taints.
11 The Story of the Monk Who Found Fault, III 376

254 There is no footprint in the sky, there is no <term>samana</term> <gloss>ascetic</gloss> outside this path. Mankind delights in the world of multiplicity, but the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>the enlightened ones</gloss> are free from multiplicity.

255 There is no footprint in the sky, there is no <term>samana</term> <gloss>ascetic</gloss> outside this path. There is no permanence in the <term>sankharas</term> <gloss>conditioned phenomena</gloss>, there is no wavering in the Buddhas.
12 The Story of the Wanderer Subhadda, III 377

XVIII THE CHAPTER ON STAINS EIGHTEENTH

<summary>This page contains verses 250 through 255 of the Dhammapada, which focus on the nature of mental stains, the difficulty of self-reflection, and the state of the enlightened. These verses are accompanied by references to their traditional narratives found in the commentary.</summary>
